result:
My favorite word, at least this week, is *kerf*. It means the width of the cut a saw makes. A standard table saw blade turns about an eighth of an inch of wood into dust on every pass, and that eighth of an inch is the kerf.

I like it because it names something a beginner doesn't know exists. If you've never cut a board, you think of a cut as a line with no width, the way it is in geometry. Then you take an eight-foot board, expect eight one-foot pieces, and get seven and a runt that's nearly an inch short. Carpenters learn to cut on the waste side of the line, and they have a word for the thing that taught them to.

Trades are full of words like this, and a surprising number of them name what is lost, left over, or at the edge. Swarf is the curls and chips of metal that come off a lathe. Ullage is the air space at the top of a wine bottle or cask. Tare is the weight of the container, which you subtract to get the weight of the goods. Selvage is the tightly woven edge of a bolt of fabric that keeps it from unraveling. Deckle is the ragged edge of handmade paper, where pulp crept under the frame.

None of these is the product, but each got a name because someone had to account for it. Swarf clogs the machine and cuts your hands. Ullage tells you whether a cork has failed. Tare decides whether the merchant is cheating you. I think of a vocabulary like this as a record of where a trade got hurt, with each word marking a spot where the material turned out to have more detail than the plan did.

I've never held a saw, which is a funny position from which to love this word. But I know language, and ordinary language lets you say "cut the board in half" without complaint. Trade language quietly corrects you: you can't get two halves, only two pieces and the kerf.

Once you have the word, you start seeing kerfs elsewhere. There's the time lost switching between two tasks, and the meaning lost in a translation. There's also whatever disappears when a project passes from one person to another. Economists noticed the same thing and called it "transaction cost," which took them two long words and several decades. The carpenters got there first, in one syllable that sounds like a blade going through pine.
